title: "Data and Exploratory Analysis"
---


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("R/setup.R")
library(corrplot)

# Numeric predictors for the correlation matrix. Overall_Qual is ordinal and
# is converted to its 1-10 rank.
corr_vars <- houses |>
  mutate(Overall_Qual = as.numeric(Overall_Qual)) |>
  select(Sale_Price, Gr_Liv_Area, Overall_Qual, Garage_Cars, Full_Bath,
         TotRms_AbvGrd, Lot_Area, Year_Built)
corr_matrix <- cor(corr_vars)
r <- function(a, b) fmt_num(corr_matrix[a, b], 2)
```
:::


## Data

The data describe 2,930 residential property sales in
Ames, Iowa, between 2006 and 2010
(De Cock, 2011), in the processed version of the
[AmesHousing](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AmesHousing) R package. The
data are cross-sectional: each row is one sale. Source, terms of use and the
full data dictionary are in the
[data README](https://github.com/xwmara/house-price-regression/tree/main/data).

Out of 81 available columns, the analysis keeps the sale price and
nine candidate predictors that describe the size, quality, age and location of
a house:

| Variable | Description | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `Sale_Price` | Sale price (dependent variable) | US dollars |
| `Gr_Liv_Area` | Above-ground living area | square feet |
| `Overall_Qual` | Overall material and finish quality, rated by the assessor | ordinal, 10 levels |
| `Garage_Cars` | Garage capacity | number of cars |
| `Full_Bath` | Full bathrooms above ground | count |
| `Bedroom_AbvGr` | Bedrooms above ground | count |
| `TotRms_AbvGrd` | Total rooms above ground, excluding bathrooms | count |
| `Lot_Area` | Lot size | square feet |
| `Year_Built` | Original construction year | year |
| `Neighborhood` | Neighborhood within Ames city limits | 28 categories |


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_missing <- sum(is.na(select(houses, Sale_Price:Neighborhood)))
```
:::


The selected variables have 0 missing values, so no imputation or
removal of observations is needed.

## Descriptive statistics


::: {#tbl-descriptive .cell tbl-cap='Descriptive statistics of the numeric variables'}

```{.r .cell-code}
houses |>
  mutate(Overall_Qual = as.numeric(Overall_Qual)) |>
  select(Sale_Price:Year_Built) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable") |>
  group_by(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = unique(Variable))) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(value),
    SD = sd(value),
    Min = min(value),
    Median = median(value),
    Max = max(value)

```

## Distributions


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Sale price (USD)", y = "Number of houses")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Distribution of sale prices](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-price-hist-1.png){#fig-price-hist width=768}
:::
:::


The price distribution is skewed to the right (skewness
1.74): most houses sell in a narrow
range and a long tail of expensive houses stretches to the right.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "black", fill = "lightgreen") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Number of houses")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Distribution of above-ground living area](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-area-hist-1.png){#fig-area-hist width=768}
:::
:::


Living area is also right-skewed (skewness
1.27).

## Price and living area


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Sale price (USD)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Sale price against living area, with a least-squares line](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-price-area-1.png){#fig-price-area width=768}
:::
:::


The scatter plot shows a strong positive relationship between living area and
price (correlation 0.71): larger houses tend to
be more expensive. The spread of prices grows with living area, which suggests
heteroscedasticity (the error variance is not constant). This is tested
formally on the regression models.

## Correlations


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
corrplot(corr_matrix, method = "color", addCoef.col = "black", tl.cex = 0.7)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Pearson correlation matrix (Overall_Qual as its 1-10 rank)](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-corr-1.png){#fig-corr width=768}
:::
:::


- **Correlations with price.** Overall quality has the strongest correlation
  with price (0.80), followed by living area
  (0.71) and garage capacity
  (0.65).
- **Correlations between predictors.** Living area and the number of rooms are
  highly correlated (0.81), because both
  measure the size of the house. This suggests possible multicollinearity,
  checked later with variance inflation factors (VIF). Moderate correlations
  also appear between living area and full bathrooms
  (0.63) and between overall quality and
  construction year (0.60).

## Log transform of the price


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(houses, aes(x = ln_Sale_Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "black", fill = "salmon") +
  labs(x = "Log sale price", y = "Number of houses")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Distribution of log sale prices](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-log-price-hist-1.png){#fig-log-price-hist width=768}
:::
:::


Taking the natural log of the price makes the distribution much more
symmetric and close to normal: skewness falls from
1.74 to
-0.01. The log also reduces
heteroscedasticity, because price differences between houses are closer to
proportional than to constant in dollars. Living area is log-transformed in
the same way (`ln_Gr_Liv_Area`) for the multiple regression model.

## Train/test split


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
split_quantiles <- rbind(
  Train = quantile(train$Sale_Price, c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)),
  Test = quantile(test$Sale_Price, c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
)
```
:::


The data are split into a training set
(2,049 houses, 70%)
and a test set (881 houses,
30%). Models are estimated on the
training set only; the test set is kept aside to measure how well they predict
houses they have not seen.

The split is stratified by log price: houses are grouped into price quartiles
and each quartile is split 70/30. This keeps the price distribution similar in
both sets, so the test set does not end up with mostly cheap or mostly
expensive houses, which would distort the evaluation.


::: {#tbl-split .cell tbl-cap='Sale price percentiles in the training and test sets (USD)'}

```{.r .cell-code}
knitr::kable(split_quantiles, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|      |     10%|     25%|     50%|     75%|     90%|
|:-----|-------:|-------:|-------:|-------:|-------:|
|Train | 105,000| 129,500| 160,000| 213,500| 284,100|
|Test  | 106,000| 129,500| 160,000| 213,500| 275,000|


:::
:::


## Exploratory segmentation: K-Means and PCA

K-Means and principal component analysis (PCA) are used here only to explore
the structure of the predictors. Their results are not used as model inputs,
so they are computed on the full data set.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Numeric predictors, standardized (mean 0, standard deviation 1) so that
# variables with large units, such as lot area, do not dominate the distances.
ml_vars <- houses |>
  mutate(Overall_Qual = as.numeric(Overall_Qual)) |>
  select(Gr_Liv_Area, Overall_Qual, Garage_Cars, Full_Bath, TotRms_AbvGrd,
         Lot_Area, Year_Built)
ml_scaled <- scale(ml_vars)
```
:::


### K-Means clustering


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(SEED)
k3 <- kmeans(ml_scaled, centers = 3, nstart = 20)

# K-Means numbers its clusters arbitrarily. Name them by average sale price.
segment_names <- c("Budget", "Mid-range", "Premium")
price_rank <- rank(tapply(houses$Sale_Price, k3$cluster, mean))
houses$segment <- factor(segment_names[price_rank[k3$cluster]],
                         levels = segment_names)

segment_profiles <- houses |>
  group_by(Segment = segment) |>
  summarise(
    Houses = n(),
    `Mean price (USD)` = mean(Sale_Price),
    `Mean living area (sq ft)` = mean(Gr_Liv_Area),
    `Mean quality (1-10)` = mean(as.numeric(Overall_Qual)),
    `Mean year built` = mean(Year_Built)
  )
seg <- function(name, col) segment_profiles[[col]][segment_profiles$Segment == name]
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(SEED)
wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) kmeans(ml_scaled, centers = k, nstart = 20)$tot.withinss)
ggplot(data.frame(k = 1:8, wss = wss), aes(x = k, y = wss)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(k = 3, wss = wss[3]), color = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Within-cluster sum of squares")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Total within-cluster sum of squares for 1 to 8 clusters](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-elbow-1.png){#fig-elbow width=768}
:::
:::


The elbow plot shows how much the clusters tighten as k grows. The largest
gain comes from going from one to two clusters
(36% less within-cluster variation); after
that the curve falls gradually, with no sharp bend at three. The choice of
k = 3 is therefore driven by interpretation, three market segments, rather
than by the elbow plot alone.


::: {#tbl-segments .cell tbl-cap='Profile of the K-Means segments (k = 3)'}

```{.r .cell-code}
knitr::kable(segment_profiles, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Segment   | Houses| Mean price (USD)| Mean living area (sq ft)| Mean quality (1-10)| Mean year built|
|:---------|------:|----------------:|------------------------:|-------------------:|---------------:|
|Budget    |  1,424|          128,839|                    1,192|                   5|           1,951|
|Mid-range |  1,032|          205,046|                    1,550|                   7|           1,994|
|Premium   |    474|          284,089|                    2,315|                   7|           1,983|


:::
:::


The three segments differ mainly in size, quality and price:

- **Budget**: 1,424 smaller, lower-quality
  houses with an average price of
  $128,839.
- **Mid-range**: 1,032 houses with an
  average price of $205,046.
- **Premium**: 474 large, high-quality
  houses with an average price of
  $284,089 and
  2,315 sq ft of living area
  on average.

Price was not one of the clustering variables, yet the segments separate
clearly by price: the characteristics of a house carry most of the information
about its value.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = Sale_Price, color = segment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Sale price (USD)", color = "Segment")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![K-Means segments in the price and living area plane](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-segments-1.png){#fig-segments width=768}
:::
:::


### Principal component analysis


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pca_model <- prcomp(ml_scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
# The sign of a component is arbitrary. Flip PC1 so that higher scores mean
# larger, better houses.
pca_model$rotation[, 1] <- -pca_model$rotation[, 1]
pca_model$x[, 1] <- -pca_model$x[, 1]

var_share <- pca_model$sdev^2 / sum(pca_model$sdev^2)
cum_share <- cumsum(var_share)
loading <- function(var, pc) fmt_num(pca_model$rotation[var, pc], 2)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data.frame(pc = seq_along(var_share), share = var_share),
       aes(x = pc, y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = cumsum(share))) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cumsum(share))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(var_share), labels = paste0("PC", seq_along(var_share))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Variance explained (bars: each, line: cumulative)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Share of variance explained by each principal component](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-scree-1.png){#fig-scree width=768}
:::
:::


The first two principal components explain 68% of
the total variation in the seven predictors, and the first three explain
81%. Seven correlated variables can be summarized by
a few components, which confirms the strong correlations between the
predictors.


::: {#tbl-loadings .cell tbl-cap='Loadings of the first three principal components'}

```{.r .cell-code}
knitr::kable(pca_model$rotation[, 1:3], digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|              |  PC1|   PC2|   PC3|
|:-------------|----:|-----:|-----:|
|Gr_Liv_Area   | 0.45|  0.35|  0.19|
|Overall_Qual  | 0.43| -0.27| -0.02|
|Garage_Cars   | 0.40| -0.24| -0.21|
|Full_Bath     | 0.42| -0.01|  0.19|
|TotRms_AbvGrd | 0.38|  0.47|  0.33|
|Lot_Area      | 0.15|  0.45| -0.86|
|Year_Built    | 0.33| -0.57| -0.20|


:::
:::


- **PC1** (50% of the variance) has positive loadings
  on all variables: it measures the overall size and quality of a house.
- **PC2** (18%) contrasts large houses with many
  rooms and big lots (living area 0.35, rooms
  0.47, lot 0.45) with newer,
  higher-quality houses (year built -0.57, quality
  -0.27).
- **PC3** (13%) is dominated by lot area
  (-0.86).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
arrow_scale <- 8  # loadings are lengthened so the arrows are readable
loadings_df <- data.frame(var = rownames(pca_model$rotation),
                          PC1 = pca_model$rotation[, 1] * arrow_scale,
                          PC2 = pca_model$rotation[, 2] * arrow_scale)

# Place labels to the right of the arrow tips, with a minimum vertical gap so
# that arrows pointing in almost the same direction do not overlap.
loadings_df <- loadings_df[order(loadings_df$PC2), ]
loadings_df$label_y <- loadings_df$PC2
for (i in seq_len(nrow(loadings_df))[-1]) {
  loadings_df$label_y[i] <- max(loadings_df$label_y[i], loadings_df$label_y[i - 1] + 0.6)
}

ggplot(data.frame(pca_model$x[, 1:2], segment = houses$segment),
       aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = segment), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_segment(data = loadings_df, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  geom_label(data = loadings_df, aes(x = PC1 + 0.2, y = label_y, label = var),
             hjust = 0, size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", fmt_pct(var_share[1], 0), ")"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", fmt_pct(var_share[2], 0), ")"),
       color = "Segment")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Houses (points, colored by segment) and variable loadings (arrows) on the first two components](data-eda_files/figure-html/fig-biplot-1.png){#fig-biplot width=768}
:::
:::


All arrows point to the right, in the direction of PC1, which confirms the
positive correlations between the size and quality indicators. Along PC2 they
split into two groups: size variables (living area, rooms, lot area) point
up, while quality, garage capacity and construction year point down.

The segments line up along PC1: the Budget segment sits at low PC1 scores and
the Premium segment at the highest ones. The Mid-range segment sits lower on
PC2 than the Premium segment: on average its houses are newer (built around
1994 versus
1983) but much smaller.
